blocks.text: Biodiversity: concept and levels

Earth is home to an astonishing variety of living things, from bacteria to blue whales. **Biodiversity** is the word for the whole variety of life on Earth, and it was popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson. It is studied at three levels.
The variety of life at all levels of biological organisation: the diversity of genes within a species, of species within a region and of ecosystems in a landscape.

blocks.caption: Three levels of biodiversity
rows: Variation in the genes within a species

The medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria shows variation in the potency and concentration of the active chemical reserpine in different regions of the Himalayas; India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and about 1,000 varieties of mango
Variety of species in a region
The Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats
Variety of ecosystems in a region
India, with deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has a greater ecosystem diversity than a country such as Norway

blocks.text: According to the IUCN (2004), over 1.5 million species have been described so far, but the real number is much larger. Robert May estimated the global total at about 7 million. More than 70 per cent of recorded species are animals, and among the animals insects are the most species-rich group, making up more than 70 per cent of the animals. Plants, including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms, make up no more than 22 per cent of the total. India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area but about 8.1 per cent of the global species diversity, so it is one of the 12 mega-diversity countries of the world.
Patterns of biodiversity

Diversity is not spread evenly over the Earth. The most important pattern is the **latitudinal gradient**: species diversity decreases as we move from the equator towards the poles. The tropics, between 23.5 degrees north and 23.5 degrees south, have more species than temperate and polar areas. For example, Colombia, which lies on the equator, has about 1,400 species of birds, New York (41 degrees north) has about 105 species and Greenland (71 degrees north) only about 56. The tropical Amazonian rain forest has the greatest biodiversity on the earth, with more than 40,000 species of plants, 3,000 of fishes, 1,300 of birds, 427 of mammals, 427 of amphibians, 378 of reptiles and over 125,000 invertebrates.

Three hypotheses have been given for the greater richness of the tropics. First, the tropics have remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years, so there has been a long **evolutionary time** for species to diversify, whereas temperate regions were subject to glaciation. Second, tropical environments are less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable, which promotes niche specialisation and greater species diversity. Third, there is more solar energy, which means higher productivity and, indirectly, greater diversity.

Another pattern is the **species-area relationship**. After studying the plants of many regions, Alexander von Humboldt found that within a region, species richness increases with the area explored, but only up to a limit. On a logarithmic scale the relationship is a straight line.

blocks.latex: \log S = \log C + Z \log A \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad S = C A^{Z}
blocks.text: S is species richness, A is the area, Z is the slope of the line (the regression coefficient) and C is the Y-intercept. Z is about 0.1 to 0.2 whatever the taxonomic group or the region, but for very large areas such as whole continents the slope is steeper, with Z between 0.6 and 1.2.

blocks.problem: In a forest, 10 hectares contain 40 species of plants, and the species-area relationship is S = C A^Z with Z = 0.2. How many species are expected in 320 hectares of the same forest?
blocks.solution: The area increases by a factor of 320 / 10 = 32. The number of species increases by the factor 32 raised to the power 0.2. Since 32 = 2^5, 32^0.2 = 2^(5 x 0.2) = 2^1 = 2. Hence the expected number of species is 40 x 2 = 80. This shows that a 32-fold increase in area only doubles the species richness, because Z is small.
blocks.answer: 80 species; a 32-fold larger area gives only twice the species.

blocks.text: Species richness falls from the equator to the poles. Z is 0.1 to 0.2 for areas within a region and 0.6 to 1.2 for whole continents. Tropical richness is explained by long evolutionary time, a constant environment and high solar energy.
Importance of biodiversity

Why does biodiversity matter? Biodiversity provides **ecosystem services**. The Amazon forest, for example, is said to produce about 20 per cent of the oxygen of the earth's atmosphere through photosynthesis. Ecosystems also pollinate plants, purify water, form soil and give aesthetic pleasure. Robert Costanza and colleagues estimated in 1997 that the services of nature are worth about 33 trillion US dollars every year, a sum far larger than the global gross national product at that time.

Ecologists have tried to explain why species richness is important. David Tilman's long-term field experiments with plots showed that the plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass and higher productivity. Paul Ehrlich's **rivet popper hypothesis** compares an ecosystem with an aeroplane in which the species are the rivets that join the parts. Loss of a few rivets may not matter at first, but loss of more and more rivets, especially of those in the crucial parts such as the wings, makes the structure unsafe. Species too differ in importance, and nobody can say in advance which loss will cause a collapse.
Causes of biodiversity loss

Biodiversity is declining quickly. In the last 500 years, 784 species (including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) have gone extinct, according to the IUCN Red List (2004). Well-known examples are the dodo of Mauritius, the quagga of Africa, the thylacine of Australia, Steller's sea cow of Russia and three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan and Caspian). The causes are summed up as the **'evil quartet'**.

**1. Habitat loss and fragmentation.** This is the most important cause. Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 per cent of the world's land surface, and now cover not more than 6 per cent. The Amazon rain forest, called the 'lungs of the planet', has been cut to grow soya beans and to raise cattle. Habitats are also broken into small patches (fragmentation) so that animals that need large territories, such as migratory birds and mammals, are badly affected.

**2. Over-exploitation.** Humans have always depended on nature for food and shelter, but when 'need' turns into 'greed' the use becomes excessive. Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon were lost for this reason, and many marine fish stocks are over-harvested today.

**3. Alien species invasions.** When alien species are introduced, some become invasive and cause the decline or extinction of native species. The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria led eventually to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish. Invasive weeds such as carrot grass (*Parthenium*), *Lantana* and water hyacinth (*Eichhornia*) have damaged our native species. The illegal introduction of the African catfish *Clarias gariepinus* for aquaculture is a threat to the indigenous catfishes of our rivers.

**4. Co-extinctions.** When a species becomes extinct, the species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct. When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique parasites also meet the same fate. Another example is the case of a coevolved plant-pollinator mutualism, where the extinction of one leads to the extinction of the other.

Remember the order for the evil quartet: habitat loss and fragmentation (the most important), over-exploitation, alien species invasion and co-extinction. In exams, the Nile perch belongs to alien species and Steller's sea cow to over-exploitation.
Approaches to biodiversity conservation
Conservation is justified on three grounds, which are called the approaches to biodiversity conservation.

blocks.caption: Reasons for conserving biodiversity
rows: Humans derive direct economic benefits from nature

Food, firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products such as tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins and perfumes, and products of medicinal importance; a large number of drugs come from plants
Biodiversity plays a major role in many ecosystem services that nature provides
Oxygen from photosynthesis, pollination, water purification, and the aesthetic pleasure of walking through a forest
Every species has an intrinsic value, even if it is of no current economic value
We have a moral duty to care for the well-being of every species and to pass on our biological legacy to future generations

blocks.text: The value that a species has in itself, independent of any use it may have for humans. The ethical argument for conservation is based on it.
In situ conservation: endemism, hotspots and sacred groves

There are two broad methods of conservation. In **in situ (on site) conservation** the whole ecosystem is protected in its natural habitat, so that all the species in it, including those not yet known, are protected. It is a better method because the species stay in the environment to which they are adapted. Protected areas such as national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves are of this kind, and in India there are many of each.

**Biodiversity hotspots** are regions with very high levels of species richness, high **endemism** (species that are confined to a region and not found anywhere else) and accelerating habitat loss. There are 34 hotspots in the world (the figure given in NCERT), and the three that cover our country are the Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and the Himalaya. Together they have a very high proportion of the world's species on a small proportion of the world's land area, so protecting them is the most economical way of protecting a large number of species.
The condition of a species being restricted to one particular region and found nowhere else, for example many amphibians of the Western Ghats.

**Sacred groves** are forest patches protected by local people because of religious and cultural traditions. In the Khasi and Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh, such groves were preserved by tradition. In Meghalaya the sacred groves are the last refuges for a large number of rare and threatened plants.
Ex situ conservation: safaris, zoological parks and cryopreservation

In **ex situ (off site) conservation**, threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and placed in special setting where they can be protected and given special care. Zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks serve this purpose. In wildlife safari parks, the animals are kept in large natural-like enclosures and visitors can see them.

Modern techniques now help. The **gametes of threatened species** can be preserved in a viable and fertile condition for long periods using **cryopreservation** techniques, in which the material is stored at very low temperature (in liquid nitrogen, at about minus 196 degrees Celsius). Eggs can later be fertilised in vitro, and plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods. Seeds of different genetic strains of crop plants and wild relatives are kept in seed banks for long-term storage.

There are also international efforts. At the Earth Summit held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, the Convention on Biological Diversity was signed. At the World Summit on Sustainable Development held in 2002 in Johannesburg, 190 countries pledged to reduce significantly the current rate of biodiversity loss by 2010.

blocks.problem: A student is asked to classify these conservation methods as in situ or ex situ and to give a reason: (i) a national park, (ii) a zoological park, (iii) a sacred grove, (iv) storing eggs of an endangered frog in liquid nitrogen.
blocks.solution: In situ conservation protects species in their natural habitat. A national park and a sacred grove are in situ because the whole ecosystem stays where it is. Ex situ conservation removes species from the natural habitat. A zoological park and storing eggs in liquid nitrogen by cryopreservation are therefore ex situ. The test is simple: ask whether the organism is protected where it naturally lives.
blocks.answer: (i) in situ, (ii) ex situ, (iii) in situ, (iv) ex situ.

blocks.problem: Tropical rain forests covered more than 14 per cent of the world's land surface earlier and now cover about 6 per cent. By what percentage has the forest cover decreased relative to the earlier cover?
blocks.solution: The decrease in cover is 14 - 6 = 8 percentage points of the land surface. Relative to the earlier cover this is 8 / 14 x 100 = 57.1 per cent. So more than half of the earlier rain forest area is gone, which is why habitat loss is the most important cause of species loss.

blocks.text: In situ: national parks, sanctuaries, biosphere reserves, hotspots and sacred groves protect the whole ecosystem. Ex situ: zoological parks, botanical gardens, safari parks, seed banks and cryopreservation protect species outside their habitat. In situ is preferred.
Common mistake: placing safari parks and cryopreservation under in situ conservation. If the species is removed from its natural habitat, it is ex situ, even if the enclosure is large.

questions.stem: Variation in the potency of the chemical reserpine in the plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different regions is an example of
questions.explanation: Variation within a single species, here in the amount and potency of reserpine in Rauwolfia vomitoria, reflects differences in genes. It is therefore genetic diversity. Species diversity concerns the number of species, and ecological diversity concerns ecosystems.

optionRationale.1: Species diversity refers to different species in a region, not variation within one species.
optionRationale.2: Ecological diversity refers to variety of ecosystems.
optionRationale.4: The variation is within one species and not between communities.

questions.stem: The pattern in which the number of species falls from the equator towards the poles is called the
questions.explanation: The latitudinal gradient in diversity means that tropical regions have more species than temperate and polar regions. Colombia near the equator has far more bird species than New York or Greenland.

optionRationale.1: The species-area relationship links species richness to the size of the area.
optionRationale.4: The rivet popper hypothesis compares species to the rivets of an aeroplane.

questions.objective: Name the latitudinal gradient of diversity

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most important cause of the loss of biodiversity?
questions.explanation: Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause of biodiversity loss. For example, tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 per cent of the land and now cover about 6 per cent. Other members of the evil quartet matter, but less so.

optionRationale.1: Co-extinction is the fourth cause of the evil quartet and less important.
optionRationale.2: Alien species invasion is important but it is not the main cause.
optionRationale.3: Genetic drift is a mechanism of evolution and not a cause of biodiversity loss in the evil quartet.

questions.objective: Recall the main cause of biodiversity loss

questions.stem: Sacred groves are best described as examples of
questions.explanation: Sacred groves are patches of forest protected by local people on religious grounds, so the species are protected in their natural habitat. This is in situ conservation. Ex situ methods include zoos, botanical gardens and cryopreservation.

optionRationale.1: Sacred groves are in the natural habitat, so they are not ex situ.
optionRationale.2: Seed banks store seeds outside the habitat.
optionRationale.4: Cryopreservation is storage at very low temperature, not a forest.

questions.objective: Classify sacred groves as in situ

questions.stem: Introduction of the Nile perch into Lake Victoria led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fishes. This is an example of loss due to
questions.explanation: The Nile perch is not native to Lake Victoria. When it was introduced, it ate or outcompeted the native cichlids, so this is an alien species invasion. It is not over-harvesting of the cichlids by humans.

optionRationale.2: The lake was not broken into patches.
optionRationale.3: Humans did not over-harvest the cichlids; the perch preyed on them.
optionRationale.4: Co-extinction is the loss of a dependent species when its partner species disappears.

questions.stem: Using S = C A^Z with Z = 0.2, if the area of a forest is increased 100 times, species richness will increase by a factor of about
questions.explanation: The factor is 100 raised to the power 0.2. Now 100^0.2 = 10^0.4 = 2.51, so the species richness increases about 2.5 times. A 100-fold increase in area therefore does not give a 100-fold increase in species.

optionRationale.1: 20 would result from multiplying 100 by Z.
optionRationale.2: 0.2 is the value of Z and not the factor.
optionRationale.4: 10 would be the factor if Z were 0.5.

questions.objective: Compute change in species richness with area

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Tropical latitudes have greater species diversity than temperate latitudes.
Reason (R): The tropical environment is less seasonal and more constant, which promotes niche specialisation.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The tropics have more species, and one accepted explanation is that tropical environments are relatively constant and predictable, which allows species to specialise in narrow niches. Along with longer evolutionary time and high solar energy, this explains the greater richness.

optionRationale.2: R is one of the explanations offered for A, so it is not an unrelated true statement.
optionRationale.3: A is true, as the latitudinal gradient shows.
optionRationale.4: R is true; tropical environments are less seasonal.

questions.stem: Match the causes of biodiversity loss in List-I with the examples in List-II.

right: II. Clearing of Amazon forest for soya bean and cattle
III. Host fish and its unique parasites
IV. Nile perch in Lake Victoria

questions.explanation: Habitat loss is illustrated by the clearing of the Amazon rain forest for soya beans and cattle (II). Over-exploitation by the loss of Steller's sea cow (I). Alien species invasion by the Nile perch in Lake Victoria (IV). Co-extinction by a host fish and its unique parasites (III). So A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

optionRationale.1: This option pairs habitat loss with Steller's sea cow.
optionRationale.3: This option pairs habitat loss with the Nile perch.
optionRationale.4: This option pairs habitat loss with the host fish and parasite.

questions.objective: Match causes of loss with examples

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about conservation.
A. In ex situ conservation, threatened species are taken out of their natural habitat.
B. Cryopreservation stores gametes of threatened species at very low temperature.
C. National parks and biosphere reserves are ex situ methods.
Choose the correct option.
questions.explanation: A and B are correct. C is wrong because national parks and biosphere reserves protect species within their natural habitat and are therefore in situ methods, whereas ex situ methods remove species from the habitat, as in zoos or cryopreservation.

optionRationale.1: C is wrong, so B and C cannot both be accepted.
optionRationale.2: C is wrong, so A and C cannot both be accepted.
optionRationale.3: C is wrong, so all three cannot be correct.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on in situ and ex situ methods

questions.stem: A biodiversity hotspot is a region that has
options: low species richness and high endemism
high species richness, high endemism and accelerating habitat loss
high species richness and no habitat loss
only high genetic diversity of crops
questions.explanation: Hotspots are defined by three features: very high species richness, high endemism (species found nowhere else) and accelerating habitat loss. Because they hold so many unique species and are under threat, they are priority areas for in situ conservation.

optionRationale.1: A hotspot has high, not low, species richness.
optionRationale.3: Hotspots face accelerating habitat loss, so loss is not absent.
optionRationale.4: Genetic diversity of crops alone does not define a hotspot; richness, endemism and habitat loss do.

questions.objective: State the criteria of a biodiversity hotspot

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The loss of a species may also cause the extinction of another species.
Reason (R): A species that is obligately associated with another, such as a unique parasite of a host or a coevolved pollinator, cannot survive without it.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: This is co-extinction. If a host fish is lost, parasites that are found only on it go with it, and a plant and its specific pollinator may disappear together. The reason correctly explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: R is the explanation of A, so the choice 'not the explanation' is wrong.
optionRationale.3: A is true, because co-extinction occurs.
optionRationale.4: R is true, because obligate partners cannot survive without each other.

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. Z is between 0.1 and 0.2 for species-area relationships within a region.
B. Z is between 0.6 and 1.2 for very large areas such as whole continents.
C. C is the slope of the regression line on a log scale.
D. S = C A^Z gives a straight line on a log-log plot.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: A, B and D are correct. Taking logs of S = C A^Z gives log S = log C + Z log A, a straight line. Z is the slope, not C. C is the intercept on the Y axis, so statement C is wrong.

optionRationale.1: C is false because Z, not C, is the slope.
optionRationale.2: C is false, so any option containing it is wrong.
optionRationale.3: C is false, and this option omits B.

questions.objective: Interpret the parameters of the species-area equation

questions.stem: In a species-area relationship with Z = 0.25 an area of 16 hectares has 30 species. How many species are expected in 4,096 hectares of a similar habitat? (Take 4096 / 16 = 256, and 256^0.25 = 4.)
questions.explanation: The area increases by 4096 / 16 = 256 times. Species increase by 256^0.25. Because 256 = 4^4, 256^0.25 = 4. Hence S = 30 x 4 = 120 species. The value 7680 comes from multiplying by 256 directly, which ignores the exponent Z.

optionRationale.1: 480 comes from multiplying by 16 instead of 4.
optionRationale.2: 30 is the original number of species, without any increase.
optionRationale.4: 7680 comes from multiplying 30 by 256 and ignoring Z.

questions.objective: Apply the species-area equation with a given Z

questions.stem: A hill-top forest patch is the last refuge for several rare plants that exist nowhere else, and local people protect it as a religious place. Which pair of terms describes it best?
questions.explanation: The plants are protected in their natural habitat, which is in situ conservation, a sacred grove. They exist nowhere else, which is endemism. The other pairs mix terms that do not apply, such as cryopreservation or alien species.

optionRationale.1: The forest is a natural habitat, so ex situ methods do not apply.
optionRationale.3: Nothing in the situation involves alien species.
optionRationale.4: A zoological park houses animals, and the case does not involve over-exploitation.

questions.objective: Apply in situ conservation and endemism to a case

questions.stem: A researcher compares two plots, one with 3 plant species and the other with 20, over several years. Following the findings of David Tilman, which result is expected?
options: The 3-species plot shows less yearly variation in biomass
Both plots show the same variation
The 20-species plot shows less yearly variation in total biomass
questions.explanation: Tilman's long-term experiments found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass, and that productivity increased with species richness. So the 20-species plot should be more stable and more productive.

optionRationale.1: The reverse is true: the plot with fewer species varies more.
optionRationale.2: The experiments showed that diversity affects stability, so the variation is not the same.
optionRationale.3: Productivity increases with the number of species, so it is not lower.
